doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Nothing but options at the Blue Note and the role of mistakes
summary: At the Blue Note with a Bosendorfer he started playing without intention; he argues for trusting the limbic system and practicing creative mistake making.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yes. There was one night we were playing at — with my West Coast trio which is my touring band. We were playing at the Blue Note in New York, a gorgeous nine foot Bosendorfer piano. First set the place was packed, I sit down at the piano, I’m looking at it and I’m thinking oh my God, I’ve got nothing but options! Nothing but options! What do I do? Since I couldn’t decide anything I just started playing and everything went fine. I could have done, I could have done anything at that moment. I had nothing but options.
And that was a positive thing for you then.
To play without intention. Without imposing yourself on the music, letting the music come out and be what it is. It takes a lot of balls.
It does. And I have had students — and I have felt this way myself — that there are so many things to choose from that that makes it more difficult.

It makes it easier, let the intuition choose. Trust your intuition, it’s never wrong. What is there you could say about your life and yourself as a person that’s always right? The limbic system is making decisions in a split, a pico. It’s making billions of decisions every picosecond. Billions. It’s so fast you can’t even think about it, the conscious brain cannot handle that. It cannot handle all that information — the amount of information the body processes when it’s awake and when it’s asleep it’s incalculable. It’s always assessing the situation constantly, monitoring, putting information, codifying things. It’s constant. It never stops. But you can’t — the brain can’t tolerate that amount of information so it doesn’t give you conscious access to it. All those decisions are kept
below the level of consciousness. Too much information, you can’t handle it consciously. Only the lower brain can do it. Alligator brain.
Is there such a thing as a mistake in improvising for you?
I used to practice creative mistake making just in case I made a mistake. I used to play wrong purposely just to see how to get out of it.
Okay but if you’re playing wrong, I think we’re going in a circle here. If you’re playing wrong on purpose but you don’t maybe call it a mistake you just call it a —
Something else. An avenue to get where I want to go. Oh my. You are a fount of fascinating theories and opinions, I’ll say that Hal.
